I am 32 years old.

My ex-wife and I have a daughter together, and we adopted our son together. Both are now 4 years old.

When we were going through our separation, I felt lost and unhappy. I was self-destructive. One day, I was so angry with everything spiraling out of control that I punched a concrete wall in a moment of overwhelming emotion. This resulted in breaking my fifth metacarpal in my right hand—the hand I worked with, played games with, and used to carry my children to bed—the hand I desperately needed to ensure I could continue providing.

Upon learning the severity of the self-inflicted damage, I became almost suicidal. Keep in mind that just a few months before this, I was the happiest man, with no history of depression or anxiety. I had never experienced anger outbursts, nor was I the type to break down and cry, but I was in a tough situation that truly prevented me from seeing the light on the other side.

With nothing better to do, I looked for a game I could play WITH ONE HAND while recovering. Somehow, I stumbled upon this game and read some of the comments. I decided it was worth a try... I must admit I didn't beat the game, nor did I play as much as some of you. In fact, I may have played this game for only a day or two. That being said, after doing so, I had a new joy and hope for life. I managed to leave behind the pain and suffering that had been thrust upon me. I could experience the joy and happiness of other people. I relaxed for 5 ♥♥♥♥ minutes listening to this music, long enough to realize that I would be okay.

After realizing this, I turned off the game and went back to work. My hand hurt a lot, but I was motivated. I stopped feeling so sorry for myself and became the father I needed to be at that moment, not the weak boy I was behaving like.

Today, I am close friends with the mother of my children. We don't fight, argue, or say hurtful things to each other. We are parents and friends.

Now I have 3 children. My third child is, wait, ALSO 4 YEARS OLD. The woman I am with was going through a very similar situation at the time of my separation, and we just unexpectedly stumbled into each other's lives. We have been dating for a year and are very happy together.

Moral of the story: you never know what life has in store for you, and if I had given up when all odds were against me, I wouldn't be where I am today. This silly little game helped me realize that.

Thank you.

I like some of the ideas of this game, but the execution is atrocious and in just one hour I grew to hate this.

Attacks feel arbitrarily slow, enemies can spam attacks while only you have to deal with "slow and deliberate" attacks. Enemies can and [b]will[/b] constantly stunlock you and hit you twenty times taking half of your health in one fell swoop with no way to prevent this at all. I regularly got attacked by things like birds flying in from off-screen so fast that I had no reasonable amount of time to react. The very first boss in the game that I fought constantly spammed arrows at times where I could not physically dodge them because they always waited until I was charging up an attack which I cannot cancel. I kept dying to them because they would spam attacks just like regular enemies did and more than half of the attacks physically could not be avoided. Sometimes I would even deflect an attack and stun my attacker but still take damage from the attack which doesn't make sense. Ranged enemies are not fun at all to fight and the game would've been immediately improved massively by entirely removing them.

Half of the mementos seemed worthless, and while I actually find the idea of gradually discovering what they do either through noticing the effects yourself or through the descriptions becoming more complete each time you acquire it, this is a massive [i]detriment[/i] to the game when these items are so poorly designed.

You are not shown on the map, and moving around them is very slow even when there's no reason for this at all. The developer claimed that a single run could last 3 hours going through the game's branching paths, but I am 100% certain this is purely because of how unreasonably slow everything is to begin with.

A top-down souls-like roguelite like this with slow and deliberate combat [i]could[/i] be interesting, but this game has been handled extremely poorly.

Even the character creation screen has weird, woke gender choices that have zero effect on the game whatsoever (not even visually). Why did this need to be included? I'm not surprised that the game that immediately opens up with virtue signaling like this ended up being garbage. Don't waste your money on this.

As the dev describes it, "This is like if The Binding of Isaac and Dark Souls got smushed together", and yes, I can confirm that this game feels exactly like that from top to bottom, the concept works incredibly well. I can't take two steps without immediately recognizing something from both of those games, such as:

-Slow-paced, methodical combat.
-Trial and error progression (minimal player guidance).
-Potions that work similarly to the pills in BOI
-Weapon infusion.
-Weapons bounce off the walls.
-Multiple unlockable characters.
-Character builds are a combination of stat leveling and the items you encounter throughout a run.

Additionally, there are many little details that add a lot to the main experience. For example, you can track your character's hunger, temperature, and even footstep noise. You can also set a whole forest on fire, and I'm pretty sure that lightning has some level of interactivity with metal objects such as shields. To call this game a hidden gem might be a bit of an understatement.

[u][b]In Celebration of Violence[/b][/u] is an incredibly deliberate, methodical, slow-paced, and ambiguous action roguelite with an extremely steep learning curve. It is not your typical fast-paced action roguelite but can instead be best likened to [u][url=https://store.steampowered.com/app/570940/DARK_SOULS_REMASTERED/]Dark Souls[/url][/u].

Overall, I recommend this game but with a few major caveats: very few things are explained to you, you will have to experiment and discover things for yourself, you will die a lot, and you will have to put in a number of hours to even begin to learn how things work. It is not a game that you will pick up instantly, nor can you button mash and expect to win — instead, you'll have to be patient and play very intelligently. It will also feel unfair for a very long time but most things in the game end up being fair once you learn how to adapt to them. If you feel like taking on a massive challenge while playing something vastly slower and more methodical than other games in the genre then I recommend it for you, otherwise steer clear of this game.

Most achievements will be acquired naturally through gameplay while a few will have to be specifically sought out; however, the [i]Loremaster[/i] achievement takes forever to get while [i]The Cursed One[/i] is luck-based. If you just play games for easy achievements then you'll want to pass on this one since you should expect to have to spend around 100+ hours to get all of the achievements (mostly due to [i]Loremaster[/i] achievement because the drop rate for the "Missing Page" items is exceedingly low).

[h3]Gameplay[/h3]
The gameplay is very deliberate and methodical: you have a limited amount of stamina which you need to manage properly otherwise you risk getting stunned and overrun, every weapon has to "wind up" before you make an attack with it (especially with heavier weapons), and your movement speed is slow. As such, the combat is very tactical and requires a tremendous amount of patience as you attempt to out-maneuver your enemies (where you are often outnumbered) and try to find an opening to get one or two attacks in before having to back off to let your stamina recharge. This isn't a fast-paced game by any means and you are certainly not overpowered compared to your enemies who (mostly) have the same limitations as you and react accordingly to each of your actions in combat; however, where they have numbers, you have brains to outwit them.

The game has two meta progression systems:
- The first allows you to level up your stats using experience which you carry out of a run; however, experience is also used as the main currency during a run so you have to consider whether you save it to level up after a run or spend it during the run.
- The second gives you permanent passive bonuses when you complete certain in-game achievements which I think is very clever. It's a great system which incentivizes you try out different characters and try to unlock the achievements.

There are a total of 19 characters, 19 randomly-generated biomes, 19 bosses, and plenty of diverse weapons, equipment, mementos, and spells:
- The characters only differ in terms of their stats and starting weapons/mementos. These statistical differences make some of them play quite differently, so you will have to change your playstyle to adapt to them, but most will end up playing similar to others which means that there isn't really as much variety as it looks like on the surface.
- The biomes provide great variety and have many unique aspects to them ranging from the availability of certain types of resources (including food), weather, and other things for you to discover.
- The bosses are all unique and enjoyable to fight, especially once you learn their patterns and can destroy them.
- The number of weapons/equipment/mementos/spells is quite large but I found myself gravitating towards whatever was strongest or most effective in order to complete runs. Moreover, the mechanical text of everything in the game is initially hidden and must be "analyzed" (or revealed) by picking them up multiple times. This is an interesting and novel system because it can help incentivize you to go out of your comfort zone and use different things and experiment; however, it is also double-edged because it doesn't respect your time as a player since it forces you to fully analyze most things in order to get to the "good" part of the game where you know what to pick and what to avoid.
- The spell system is unintuitive and obtuse: each use of a spell consumes your experience which I don't think works well because experience is already used as currency. This system also limits the amount of spells you can use which somewhat forces you to rely on weapons rather than be able to play a full spellcaster.

[h3]Graphics[/h3]
The graphics use cute pixel art which serves the game well, though they belie the game's true nature.

[h3]Sound[/h3]
The music uses purely atmospheric tracks which tend to suit the mood of the biome you're in or the boss you're facing but I found them quite uninspiring and boring (some even bordering on grating) so I ended up listening to my own music most of the time.

[h3]Story[/h3]
The story is largely unexplained and you won't even be able to begin to understand the enigmatic world unless you collect most of the 165 "Missing Page" items which are very rare drops. Even if you do collect all of them, the world will still be shrouded in ambiguity due to their nature but you'll see that the world-building is deeper than it first seems. The story also has a few neat metaphors and twists here and there (if you can find them).

[h3]Conclusion[/h3]
Overall, I recommend this game but only if you're willing to put the time in. If you don't want to spend a number of hours learning how the game works first then it won't be for you. Otherwise, this is a great game to get sucked into if you like a slower-paced challenge and enjoy discovering things with wide-eyed awe.

As I write the describer 'unfairly overlooked' I do wonder, is it unfair to be overlooked? Is that even bad...? Not sure. Maybe it's even good sometimes.

Been playing Steam games for years. I think roguelikes are the most fun sort of game to have come out of the Steam 'thing' in the last ten years.

This was, maybe, the most fun I've had. Which is crazy to say in a world that has Nuclear Throne and Dead Cells, but there you go. And so few people know about this game! I mean, unless I'm missing something, shouldn't this game be as big as Dead Cells?(I know, that's a reach...) I had way more fun with this game than Celeste or Spelunky(not saying the latter isn't way, way influential). I know the lore is weird and obtuse. I know a single run takes too long. But this game was worth it. It should've been big. It had a weird, Disco Elysium otherness to its world building. It had a dark, skeptical take on bloodshed and the medieval types of worlds that people always gladly hack and pillage their way through. It had cool physics. It had an awesome assortment of characters you could be- including unheroic types and holy types, I know maybe that's been done before but still great. The roguelike elements in this game actually felt unpredictable and made for strange outcomes. If I think of the 'weird' 10/10 type of games on Steam or in the indieverse... Lisa the Painful, Barkley Shut Up and Jam Gaiden, Frog Fractions, Dwarf Fortress, Caves of Qud... all of these games either sold a lot or were huge on Reddit, forums, youtube. This game barely appeared on any of those sites. At all. HOW? This game maybe isn't as original as some of the games. But it's as GOOD, FUN and almost as weird. ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥. (might not fit the the theological underpinnnings, leanings of the game. Or maybe everyone has been damned by God in In Celebration of Violence.)

Devs, reviewers, indie game fans should've gotten so much more behind this. Reviewers and Indie fans every year back and buy weirdo products like Doki Doki and Pathologic and... you name it. Why couldn't this have been highlighted too?

I'll say it again: unfairly overlooked is not necessarily bad. Fairly looked at and you're a Mario Kart game. Who wants to be that? I mean, would you rather be Bad Brains or Green Day? Would you rather be God Shammgod or Steph Curry? Would you rather be a Laika movie or a Pixar movie? Would you rather be beautiful or popular? I know, I know if you're Beyonce or Bjork you can be both. But sometimes you can only be one of those.

The dev has put out two more games after this which seem like they are similarly great but perhaps more modest/less strange, Thy Kingdom Crumble and Tanklike. The former, a Downwell-like with a cool, completely out-of-place rising, looking upward, beatific, stained glass, Catholic aesthetic and the latter, a characterless tank battle game. It means that people didn't respond or couldn't understand the gaps, the unexplainings, the originality of In Celebration of Violence. Too bad for us.

This isn't like Rain World, a brilliant, unfun game. Rain World you die and you want to slit your wrists- this game you die and it's bracing and thrilling. This is a brilliant, fun game that people should buy and play now. Or just buy and help the dev make more games. And maybe you don't even need to make more games. Do you need more than one Bad Brains?

This feels like the kind of game a distant friend of yours recommends you with the warning "Don't give up at the start, it gets better!".

You then play through the whole thing wondering exactly when it gets better, until you realize you've beaten it.

Such an incredibly cool name too...

To be fair, I have stuck through games that make terrible first impressions before, and found that they were great, but In Celebration of Violence did not exactly give me that kind of motivation, probably because it has a soundtrack that would be more stimulating if it was replaced entirely by YouTube Minecraft mod review background music from 2012, and a main character who seems to simultaneously have insomnia and exist in a constant state of Melatonin overdose, judging by the speed at which they do literally anything.

Granted, if you're the kind of person who likes your combat VERY slow [spoiler] (Only for you, that is. The archer enemies will use quantum translocation technology to make 14 arrows appear inside your liver in the span of about 0.5 seconds.) [/spoiler] and VERY deliberate and like games where encountering multiple birds at once is deadlier than having a battleaxe plunged directly into your stomach this is probably the game for you.

Eh, I'd give it a mixed rating, but for a very low discount price, there is a good chunk of fun to squeeze from it.

The game is a roguelite, with different currencies, used for trading, leveling and crafting, different potions to be thrown and used, different passive artifacts, different spells, and naturally different weapons and environments. The variety is pretty damn large, so there is a really big potential timesink to find here.
You will quickly realize that the combat is very deliberate and punishing, if you find any tools that help with cheesing encounters, you better damn use them. As soon as you have no cheese at hand, you will need to always keep in mind the stamina bar. Stamina is a god of combat here, it's used for dodges, blocks and attacks, and all of thes actions use a LOT of stamina. You can try playing risky, but without having the timings down to milliseconds, it will probably not take you far.
You can avoid some encounters, but without XP and/or cheese, you will not be able to defeat the bosses (who all have minions).
It sounds pretty damn interesting, and for a long time it is, however with the sheer amount of threats on screen, it really comes down to crowd control, dodging some bullet hells, and punishing after parries where possible.
The game mentions our good ol friend dArk SoUlS, which always irks me in context of roguelikes, as the encounters are not designed worth S**T, there isn't a clever level design, no intricate movesets that work like ballet against yours, it's just combo of "Losable currency+stamina+hard+slower pace", which I'd throw to trash if it's used as a basis to draw comparison to DS.
When I played ICoV, it reminded me mostly of mobile's Pixel Dungeon, both visually, and with how the roguelite progression feels, even though they play completely different. Ever since I completed TBoI and Rogue Legacy, the roguelite formula on its own has grown stale for me, making me always look for what works well with it, and what works against it. ICoV doesn't shake the core design at all, it's a very "by the book" roguelite in terms of progression and "most" mechanics, it didn't shock me beyond a simple "oh, that's neat", like with f.e. forest fires, power mechanics that allow to crush different items with main weapon, slowly filling out descriptions as you defeat enemies or pick up items, certain spell interactions etc.

Story is kind of interesting, though as my patience ran its course, I unfortunately couldn't see its conclusion, leaving me with the story from intro, and less so interesting lore snippets. What you need to know is that for tens of hours, the main story will not be hugely affecting your gameplay.

Audio is decent, especially how satisfying the "clang" is when parrying, it's quiet for the most part, with recognizable sound effects in the background, and only minimal music. I was not blown away, but it was most importantly functional.

Visuals are so generic it drains my soul, pixel count is so low, and color choices so limited, that any and all detail is flushed down the drain. You have some modern vfx to spice it up, and line of sight mechanic, but it doesn't help it much. Experience may vary from person to person, but for me the looks were so tiring, ugly and uninspired, that I'd rather look at ASCII graphics instead, like nethack or dwarf fortress.

Despite my negativity, I poured a good amount of hours into it, the mechanics in part have pretty damn good implementation, and planning for encounters or responding to them was exciting, but in my experience not enough to help me through many more hours to complete it, the problem with getting better at a RL game, is that playing early levels is like you're on an autopilot, and with how little change of pace I felt from even new levels being introduced, I eventually started to always play it on autopilot, with nothing ever surprising me. Even the content I didn't play, from gameplays I've seen, only looks like more of the same to me, but for a 75-90% off, you really can't go wrong with trying it out, especially if you don't get burnt out like me.

A good game. Unforgiving gameplay mixed with a lack of proper tutorial means that you either need to learn by yourself or look on the wiki. You are supposed to learn mechanics and figure out things as you play. There is some sort of in game codex; however, you unlock entries very slowly by picking up the related item. 

After each run, you get a currency with which you can either upgrade some stats or purchase/upgrade weapons at the starting zone. However, you get very little of that currency unless you get a very good run.

The bosses are all quite easy, unless you are unlucky or are fighting one specific boss in the castle, which is far more difficult than any other boss. The difficulty comes from the game spawning normal enemies along with the boss. 

Some enemies are bs, but eventually, you will learn how to avoid them somewhat and only take one hit of damage from them. Or get strong enough to smash them to pieces.

Enjoyable and unique enough to be played over other similar bigger games. I would recommend it if you
a) Like those kind of games
b) Are ready to deal with some bs
c) Are ready to learn the game by doing multiple runs
d) Are going to play the game for more than one run
